chapters.title: Rent vs. Buy: The Real Question

lessons.title: What Actually Changes When You Buy

blocks.robotComment: Buying a home changes more than just where your money goes each month. Let's map out what actually shifts. 🏠
blocks.body: When you rent, a landlord owns the property, handles most repairs, and takes on the risk if the property's value drops. When you buy, ownership shifts to you: you build equity as you pay down the loan, but you also take on the responsibility, the risk, and the costs that used to be the landlord's problem.

highlights.text: ownership shifts to you
you build equity

blocks.body: Owning means you can renovate, paint, or make a space genuinely your own without asking permission — but it also means when the water heater breaks, there's no landlord to call. Every repair, every maintenance cost, and every property value swing is now something you carry directly.

highlights.text: you carry directly

blocks.sentence: When you buy instead of rent, responsibility for repairs and maintenance generally shifts from the landlord to ___.
options: you
the bank
the government
blocks.explanation: Ownership comes with control, but also with direct responsibility for costs a landlord would otherwise have covered.

blocks.robotComment: This track isn't 'buying is better' or 'renting is better' — it's genuinely about which fits your actual situation. ⚖️
blocks.body: Neither renting nor buying is universally better — this track will make the case for both sides honestly, including in the very next lesson. The right choice depends heavily on how long you plan to stay, your local market, your finances, and how much you value flexibility versus stability.

highlights.text: depends heavily on how long you plan to stay

blocks.question: What is one of the biggest practical differences between renting and buying?
options: Responsibility for repairs and maintenance generally shifts to the owner when you buy
Renters are legally required to renovate their unit
Buying always costs less per month than renting
Owners never have to pay for anything related to the property
blocks.explanation: A landlord typically absorbs repair and maintenance responsibility for a renter — an owner takes that on directly.

blocks.statement: Buying a home is universally the better financial choice compared to renting, in every situation.
blocks.explanation: Which is better genuinely depends on the situation — timeline, market, finances, and personal priorities all matter, which is exactly what this track explores.

blocks.robotComment: The mortgage payment is just the headline number. The real cost of owning has several more lines underneath it. 🧾
blocks.body: A mortgage payment is usually the most visible cost of owning, but it's far from the only one. Property taxes, homeowners insurance, ongoing maintenance, and occasional bigger repairs all add up on top of it — and unlike rent, these costs generally aren't fixed or predictable month to month.

highlights.text: far from the only one

blocks.body: A commonly used rule of thumb is that ongoing maintenance and repairs average around 1% of a home's value per year, though this varies a lot by the home's age and condition. On a $300,000 home, that's roughly $3,000 a year on average — some years much less, some years (a new roof, a broken furnace) far more.

code.code:
Home value: $300,000
1% annual maintenance estimate: $3,000/year (≈$250/month average)

Real pattern: often $0 some years, $10,000+ other years —
the 1% is a long-run average, not a monthly bill.
code.caption: This 1% figure is a widely used rule of thumb, not a guaranteed or precise number for any specific home.

blocks.sentence: A common rule of thumb estimates ongoing maintenance costs at roughly ___% of a home's value per year, on average.
blocks.explanation: The 1%-per-year rule is a widely used, rough estimate for long-run average maintenance costs, not a precise monthly figure.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly why 'can I afford the mortgage' is the wrong question — 'can I afford owning' is the real one. 🔍
blocks.body: Because these costs are lumpy and unpredictable — a big expense can arrive with little warning — a common mistake is budgeting only for the mortgage payment and being caught off guard by everything else. A more complete plan sets aside a little each month, even when nothing is currently broken, specifically for these costs.

highlights.text: budgeting only for the mortgage payment

blocks.question: Besides the mortgage payment, what are some of the other ongoing costs of owning a home?
options: Property taxes, homeowners insurance, and maintenance/repairs
Nothing else — the mortgage payment covers everything
Only a one-time cost paid at closing
Costs that a landlord would still cover
blocks.explanation: Owning brings several ongoing costs beyond the mortgage itself, several of which don't arrive on a predictable monthly schedule.

blocks.statement: Home maintenance and repair costs tend to arrive in a smooth, predictable amount every single month.
blocks.explanation: These costs are often lumpy — some years very little, other years a large unexpected expense — which is exactly why budgeting only for the mortgage is risky.

lessons.title: When Renting Is Actually the Smarter Move

blocks.robotComment: Renting isn't 'throwing money away' — that's one of the most common myths in personal finance. Let's retire it. 🚫💸
blocks.body: Renting gets unfairly dismissed as "throwing money away," but that framing ignores what renting actually buys: flexibility, predictable costs, and freedom from the upfront and ongoing costs of ownership covered in the last lesson. For the right situation, renting isn't a consolation prize — it's genuinely the smarter financial move.

highlights.text: flexibility, predictable costs, and freedom

blocks.body: Mobility is one of the clearest cases: someone who expects to move within a few years for work, relationships, or simply uncertainty about where they want to live faces real risk in buying, since selling a home soon after buying often means eating closing costs and possibly selling before the property has appreciated enough to cover them.

highlights.text: Mobility is one of the clearest cases

blocks.sentence: Someone who expects to move again within just a few years generally faces more ___ buying a home than renting.
options: risk
flexibility
equity
blocks.explanation: A short timeline increases the risk that selling costs and market timing eat into or erase any benefit from having bought.

blocks.robotComment: There's also an opportunity-cost angle here — money not tied up in a down payment can go to work elsewhere. 💡
blocks.body: There's also an opportunity cost angle: the large sum typically needed for a down payment could instead be invested, potentially growing faster than the local real estate market over the same period, depending on the market and timing. Renting keeps that money liquid and working elsewhere, rather than tied up in one illiquid asset.

highlights.text: opportunity cost

blocks.question: Why can a short expected timeline in one place make renting the smarter financial choice?
options: Selling soon after buying often means eating closing costs before the home has appreciated enough to offset them
Renting always costs more than buying, so it doesn't matter either way
Landlords are legally required to lower rent for short-term tenants
Homes never lose value regardless of timeline
blocks.explanation: A short ownership window raises the risk that the upfront and transaction costs of buying aren't recovered before selling again.

blocks.statement: Renting is always a worse financial decision than buying, regardless of someone's situation.
blocks.explanation: For the right situation — especially a shorter expected timeline or a strong preference for flexibility — renting can genuinely be the smarter financial move.

chapters.title: How a Mortgage Payment Actually Works

blocks.robotComment: Same bill every month, completely different mix hiding inside it. 🔀
blocks.body: Every mortgage payment is actually two payments stitched together: interest, which is the cost of borrowing the money, and principal, which is the actual amount you're paying back toward what you borrowed. Even though the total payment on a fixed-rate mortgage typically stays the same every month, how it's split between the two shifts constantly.

highlights.text: interest, which is the cost of borrowing the money
principal, which is the actual amount you're paying back

blocks.body: Interest is calculated each month based on the loan's current remaining balance, not the original amount you borrowed — so as the balance shrinks, so does the dollar amount of interest charged, even at the exact same rate. Principal is simply whatever's left of the payment after that month's interest is covered.

highlights.text: based on the loan's current remaining balance

blocks.body: Here's what that looks like on a $200,000 loan at a 6% fixed annual rate over 30 years, where the monthly payment works out to roughly $1,199.10. In the very first month, the entire remaining balance is still $200,000, so interest takes a large bite before principal gets anything.

highlights.text: roughly $1,199.10

code.code:
Loan: $200,000 | Rate: 6% fixed | Term: 30 years
Monthly payment: ≈$1,199.10

Month 1 interest: $200,000 × (6% ÷ 12) = $1,000.00
Month 1 principal: $1,199.10 − $1,000.00 = $199.10
code.caption: Illustrative example — actual payments depend on the exact rate, term, and lender rounding.

blocks.sentence: Each month's interest charge is calculated based on the loan's current remaining ___, not the original loan amount.
options: balance
term
rate
blocks.explanation: Interest is charged on whatever principal is still outstanding, so it shrinks as the balance shrinks.

blocks.robotComment: Fixed payment, moving target underneath it — that's the whole story of amortization. 📉
blocks.body: Because interest is calculated on the shrinking balance, the principal portion of each payment quietly grows every single month, even though the total payment amount doesn't change. Early payments are mostly interest; late payments are mostly principal — the next lesson on amortization walks through exactly how far that shift goes.

highlights.text: the principal portion of each payment quietly grows every single month

blocks.question: Why does the dollar amount of interest charged on a fixed-rate mortgage change from month to month, even though the rate itself doesn't?
options: Interest is calculated on the current remaining balance, which shrinks a little every month
The lender randomly adjusts the interest amount
Interest is only charged in the first year of the loan
The monthly payment amount changes every month
blocks.explanation: As the balance goes down, the dollar amount of interest calculated against it goes down too, even at an unchanged rate.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly the risk side of amortization — a fixed payment hiding a moving split. ⚖️
blocks.statement: On a fixed-rate mortgage, the portion of each payment that goes toward principal stays exactly the same amount every single month.
blocks.explanation: The payment total stays the same, but the principal portion actually grows a little each month as the interest portion shrinks.

blocks.robotComment: Same math as last lesson, but now the rate itself can move underneath it. 📈📉
blocks.body: A fixed-rate mortgage locks in the same interest rate for the entire loan term, so the principal-and-interest portion of the payment never changes, no matter what happens to interest rates in the wider economy. An adjustable-rate mortgage, often called an ARM, starts with a rate that can later move up or down based on broader market conditions.

highlights.text: A fixed-rate mortgage locks in the same interest rate for the entire loan term
adjustable-rate mortgage

blocks.body: Adjustable-rate mortgages typically offer a lower interest rate during an initial fixed period, which can make the early payments noticeably cheaper than a comparable fixed-rate loan. After that initial period ends, the rate adjusts periodically based on a market index, and the payment adjusts along with it — up or down, depending on where rates have moved.

highlights.text: lower interest rate during an initial fixed period

blocks.body: The trade-off comes down to who's carrying the risk of future rate changes. Here's a simplified comparison of what the same loan amount can cost at two different rates.

highlights.text: who's carrying the risk of future rate changes

code.code:
Loan: $200,000 over 30 years

At a 4% rate: payment ≈ $955/month
At a 7% rate: payment ≈ $1,331/month

Same loan amount, same term — just comparing the payment
at the lower initial ARM-style rate versus a rate it could
adjust to later.
code.caption: Illustrative comparison only — a real ARM recalculates against the remaining balance and remaining term when it adjusts, not the original loan amount.

blocks.sentence: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate for the entire loan term, while an ___ mortgage can change after an initial period.
options: adjustable-rate
interest-only
government-backed
blocks.explanation: ARM stands for adjustable-rate mortgage — its rate can move after an initial fixed period ends.

blocks.robotComment: The real question isn't which is cheaper today — it's how long you'll actually be holding the loan. ⏳
blocks.body: Neither structure is universally right. A fixed rate trades a potentially higher starting rate for total predictability, which matters most to someone planning to stay long enough for a rate move to matter. An ARM trades that predictability for a lower starting cost, which can make sense for someone who expects to sell or refinance before the rate ever adjusts.

highlights.text: A fixed rate trades a potentially higher starting rate for total predictability
An ARM trades that predictability for a lower starting cost

blocks.question: What is the core trade-off between a fixed-rate mortgage and an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM)?
options: A fixed rate offers predictability, while an ARM offers a potentially lower initial rate in exchange for the risk of it rising later
Fixed-rate mortgages are illegal in most places
An ARM guarantees a lower total cost no matter what
There's no real difference between the two
blocks.explanation: Fixed-rate loans trade a possibly higher starting rate for certainty, while ARMs trade that certainty for a lower starting rate and future rate risk.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly the risk side of the ARM trade-off — it can cut both ways. ⚖️
blocks.statement: An adjustable-rate mortgage's interest rate can only ever move in the borrower's favor after the initial period ends.
blocks.explanation: An ARM's rate can move either up or down after the initial period, based on the market index it's tied to — it isn't guaranteed to favor the borrower.

blocks.robotComment: Same $1,199.10 payment every single month for 30 years straight — the story is entirely in how it's divided. 📊
blocks.body: An amortization schedule is just the full month-by-month record of how a loan's fixed payment splits between interest and principal, from the very first payment to the very last. The last lesson showed the two ends of that story — now here's what the middle actually looks like.

highlights.text: amortization schedule

blocks.body: Take that same $200,000 loan at a fixed 6% rate over 30 years. The payment stays at roughly $1,199.10 every month without exception, but look at how differently that same $1,199.10 gets divided depending on where the loan is in its life.

highlights.text: stays at roughly $1,199.10 every month without exception

code.code:
Loan: $200,000 | Rate: 6% fixed | Term: 30 years | Payment: $1,199.10/mo (constant)

Payment #1    (balance: $200,000.00) → Interest $1,000.00 | Principal $199.10
Payment #181  (balance: $142,097.98) → Interest   $710.49 | Principal $488.61
Payment #349  (balance:  $13,933.23) → Interest    $69.67 | Principal $1,129.43

The monthly payment never changes — only the mix inside it does.
code.caption: Illustrative fixed-rate amortization schedule for a $200,000, 6%, 30-year loan — real schedules vary slightly by lender rounding conventions.

blocks.sentence: On a fixed-rate mortgage, the total monthly payment stays constant, but the split between interest and ___ shifts throughout the loan.
options: principal
term
insurance
blocks.explanation: Amortization describes exactly how that interest/principal split moves over the life of a fixed-payment loan.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly why paying extra toward principal early in a mortgage has an outsized effect. 🎯
blocks.body: By payment #181, roughly 15 years in, the balance has only dropped from $200,000 to about $142,098 — less than a third of the original loan, even though half the term is gone. That's the front-loaded nature of interest: it takes the biggest bite early, when the remaining balance is largest, so principal barely dents the total for a long stretch.

highlights.text: less than a third of the original loan, even though half the term is gone

blocks.question: Why does the interest portion of a fixed mortgage payment shrink so much by the later years of the loan?
options: Because interest is calculated on the remaining balance, and by then the balance has shrunk substantially
Because the lender lowers the interest rate automatically over time
Because the payment amount increases in later years
Interest never actually changes throughout the loan
blocks.explanation: As the balance shrinks year after year, the interest calculated against it shrinks too, leaving a bigger share of the fixed payment for principal.

blocks.robotComment: Flip the schedule upside down and it's basically mirrored: mostly interest becomes mostly principal. 🔁
blocks.statement: In a typical fixed-rate amortization schedule, the earliest payments are weighted more heavily toward interest than the final payments are.
blocks.explanation: Interest is highest when the balance is highest, near the start of the loan, then steadily gives way to principal as the balance shrinks.

options: adjustable-rate
interest-only
variable-term

questions.question: Why are the earliest payments on a fixed-rate mortgage weighted so heavily toward interest?
options: Because interest is calculated on the remaining balance, which is largest at the start of the loan
Because lenders charge a special first-year penalty
Because principal isn't allowed to be paid in the first year
Interest is actually highest at the very end of the loan

questions.statement: On a typical fixed-rate amortization schedule, the total monthly payment amount changes from month to month.

lessons.title: Down Payments: How Much Is Enough?

blocks.robotComment: This is where 'how much house can I afford' turns into 'how much cash should I actually put down.' 💰
blocks.body: A down payment is the upfront cash you pay toward a home's purchase price, with the rest covered by the mortgage loan. The bigger the down payment, the smaller the loan — which sounds simple, but the actual trade-offs go well beyond just the size of the monthly payment.

highlights.text: A down payment is the upfront cash you pay toward a home's purchase price

blocks.body: A larger down payment means borrowing less, which lowers the monthly payment, reduces the total interest paid over the life of the loan, and can sometimes unlock better loan terms. The trade-off is that the cash goes into an illiquid asset — one that can't easily be turned back into cash — instead of staying available for emergencies, other goals, or investing elsewhere.

highlights.text: reduces the total interest paid over the life of the loan

blocks.body: Here's what that trade-off can look like on a $300,000 home financed at a fixed 6% rate over 30 years, comparing a 20% down payment to a much smaller 5% down payment.

highlights.text: a 20% down payment to a much smaller 5% down payment

code.code:
Home price: $300,000 | Rate: 6% fixed | Term: 30 years

20% down ($60,000) → Loan $240,000 → Payment ≈ $1,438.92/mo
5% down ($15,000)  → Loan $285,000 → Payment ≈ $1,708.72/mo

Over the full 30-year term, the smaller down payment path
costs roughly $52,000 more in total interest — on top of the
$45,000 difference in how much was actually borrowed.
code.caption: Illustrative comparison at one hypothetical rate — actual loan terms, rates, and minimum down payment requirements vary widely by lender, loan type, and location.

blocks.sentence: A larger down payment reduces the size of the loan, which lowers both the monthly payment and the total ___ paid over the life of the loan.
options: interest
principal
insurance
blocks.explanation: Borrowing less means less interest accrues over the loan's term, since interest is calculated on the outstanding balance.

blocks.robotComment: The biggest down payment possible isn't automatically the smartest one — reserves matter too. 🛟
blocks.body: There's no single down payment percentage that's enough for everyone — required minimums vary a lot by loan type, lender, and location, and the right amount also depends on how much cash reserve someone wants to keep on hand for emergencies and other costs of owning covered in earlier lessons. Putting down every available dollar can leave someone dangerously short on cash the moment something breaks.

highlights.text: There's no single down payment percentage that's enough for everyone

blocks.question: What is a real trade-off of putting down as large a down payment as possible?
options: It can leave less cash available as a reserve for emergencies and the ongoing costs of owning
It always guarantees a lower interest rate no matter what
It has no effect on the monthly payment at all
It eliminates the need for homeowners insurance
blocks.explanation: Putting more cash into the down payment reduces the loan and interest cost, but it also reduces how much cash is left on hand for reserves and other needs.

blocks.robotComment: If a rule of thumb sounds universal in real estate, it's almost always a starting point, not a rule. 🧭
blocks.statement: There is one universally correct down payment percentage that applies to every buyer, loan type, and situation.
blocks.explanation: Minimum requirements and the right amount to put down both vary by loan type, lender, location, and a buyer's own cash reserve needs.

blocks.robotComment: The name makes it sound like it protects the buyer — it doesn't. 🔍
blocks.body: Private mortgage insurance, usually shortened to PMI, is insurance that protects the lender — not you — against the risk of the loan defaulting. It typically gets added to the monthly payment when the down payment falls below a certain threshold, commonly cited around 20% of the purchase price, though the exact rules vary by lender and loan type.

highlights.text: protects the lender — not you
around 20% of the purchase price

blocks.body: PMI exists because a smaller down payment means the lender is financing a larger share of the home's value, which raises the lender's risk if the borrower stops paying and the home has to be sold. PMI doesn't cancel that risk for the borrower — it simply compensates the lender for taking it on, at the borrower's expense.

highlights.text: compensates the lender for taking it on, at the borrower's expense

blocks.body: PMI is usually priced as a percentage of the loan amount per year, and it gets folded into the monthly payment. Here's a simplified illustration of what that can add.

highlights.text: gets folded into the monthly payment

code.code:
Loan amount: $250,000
Illustrative PMI rate: 0.75% per year

Annual PMI cost: $250,000 × 0.75% = $1,875/year
Added to the monthly payment: ≈ $156.25/month

This is on top of the loan's regular principal and interest.
code.caption: PMI rates and rules vary significantly by lender and loan type — this is a simplified illustration, not a quoted rate.

blocks.sentence: PMI is insurance that primarily protects the ___ against the risk of the loan defaulting, not the borrower.
options: lender
borrower
government
blocks.explanation: Despite being paid by the borrower, PMI exists to protect the lender's financial interest if the loan goes unpaid.

blocks.robotComment: Worth checking in on, not just setting and forgetting — PMI removal usually isn't automatic. ✅
blocks.body: PMI usually isn't permanent. Once enough equity has built up in the home — through paying down the loan, the home appreciating in value, or both — many lenders allow it to be removed, though the specific process and threshold vary by lender and loan type. It's worth understanding as an added cost tied to the size of the down payment, not a fixed feature of every mortgage.

highlights.text: PMI usually isn't permanent

blocks.question: Who does PMI primarily protect?
options: The lender, against the risk of the loan defaulting
The borrower, against losing their job
The home itself, against physical damage
The real estate agent's commission
blocks.explanation: PMI compensates the lender for the added risk of a smaller down payment — it isn't insurance protecting the borrower.

blocks.robotComment: One more reason a bigger down payment (or building equity fast) can quietly save real money. 💡
blocks.statement: PMI is typically a permanent cost that stays on a mortgage payment for the entire life of the loan, no matter what.
blocks.explanation: PMI can usually be removed once enough equity has built up, though the exact threshold and process vary by lender and loan type.

blocks.robotComment: One of these is a rough guess. The other is a lender actually checking the numbers. 🔎
blocks.body: Pre-qualification and pre-approval sound like the same thing, but they carry very different weight when house-hunting. Pre-qualification is typically a quick, informal estimate based on financial information the buyer simply reports, without the lender verifying any of it.

highlights.text: Pre-qualification is typically a quick, informal estimate

blocks.body: Pre-approval goes several steps further: the lender actually verifies income, credit history, debts, and assets, and issues a conditional commitment for a specific loan amount, subject to a few final checks like an appraisal of the actual home chosen. It takes more paperwork and time upfront, but it means the number attached to it is far more reliable.

highlights.text: the lender actually verifies income, credit history, debts, and assets

blocks.sentence: Unlike pre-qualification, pre-approval involves the lender actually ___ a buyer's financial information before issuing a conditional commitment.
options: verifying
estimating
guessing
blocks.explanation: Verification — actually checking income, credit, and assets — is what separates pre-approval from a simple pre-qualification estimate.

blocks.robotComment: Showing up with only a pre-qualification in a competitive market is like bringing an estimate to a negotiation that wants proof. 📄
blocks.body: This distinction matters most once house-hunting actually starts. In a competitive market, sellers often favor or even require an offer backed by pre-approval, since it signals the buyer's financing is far more likely to actually come through. Pre-qualification is a reasonable starting point for a very early budget check, but it rarely carries much weight once an offer is on the table.

highlights.text: sellers often favor or even require an offer backed by pre-approval

blocks.question: What is the key difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?
options: Pre-approval involves the lender actually verifying financial information; pre-qualification is typically just a self-reported estimate
They are legally required to mean the exact same thing
Pre-qualification always results in a larger loan amount
Pre-approval has no expiration and never requires updating
blocks.explanation: Verification is the core difference — pre-approval carries far more weight because a lender has actually checked the numbers behind it.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly why house hunters are often told 'get pre-approved first.' 🏁
blocks.statement: In a competitive housing market, sellers generally treat a pre-qualification and a pre-approval as equally strong signals from a buyer.
blocks.explanation: Because pre-approval reflects actual verification, sellers typically trust it more than an unverified pre-qualification estimate.
